Input: Where does the concept of the Earth being six thousand years old come from? Is it from the Bible? It really does come from the Bible, if a bit indirectly. There are several passages in the Bible that give information on such things as how old people were when they had children or how long certain periods lasted, that if accepted at face value, can give a very close approximation of when Adam and Eve were created (according to the stories, at least). There are a few places where things get somewhat murky, but not enough to change things by more than a few decades* – nothing on the order of millions or billions of years. This was a fairly well accepted interpretation for generations, and many scholars made their own estimates of when creation would have taken place, including Johannes Kepler. Arguably the most respected of these was the estimate done by James Ussher, who put much effort into sorting out the murky periods. It's because Ussher's chronology was so well respected that it was included in the introductory material to several printed Bibles, including the famed Scofield Bible. Wikipedia gives a good summary of how Ussher made his estimate (Ussher chronology - Wikipedia). He broke it down into three periods: Using other sources outside the Bible, Ussher determined the enthronement of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk to have occurred in 562 BC, which was tied in to the end of the Babylonian Captivity through 2 Kings 25:27. From there, it was just a matter of going backwards by all the years previously calculated, putting creation at 4004 BC. Creation to Exodus You can easily look up Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 for yourself, but to give an idea, here's the start of Genesis 5: This is the list of the descendants of Adam. When God created humans,[a] he made them[b] in the likeness of God. 2 Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called them humans[c] when they were created. 3 When Adam had lived one hundred thirty years, he became the father of a son in his likeness, according to his image, and named him Seth. 4 The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he had other sons and daughters. 5 Thus all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, and he died. 6 When Seth had lived one hundred five years, he became the father of Enosh. 7 Seth lived after the birth of Enosh eight hundred seven years and had other sons and daughters. 8 Thus all the days of Seth were nine hundred twelve years, and he died. It goes on and on like that. So, as long as you accept these statements as true, it's mostly a simple matter of adding up how old each man was when he begat his heir. The only real hiccups are between Noah and Shem, and between Nahor and Terah. Both of these are somewhat ambiguous. In the former, the passage states, "After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth." In the latter, the passage is, "When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran." People who care about this issue more than I do have gone into detail to try to pinpoint those ages (e.g. Contradictions: Noah’s Three Sons). You also need to know how old Abraham was when the Exodus occurred. His age at the start of all those events comes from Genesis 12:4, "So Abram went, as the Lord had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran." I ran the math myself with a spreadsheet, and came up with 2049 years from the creation of Adam to the birth of Abraham, plus another 75 years until the Exodus, for 2124 years total (a bit different from Ussher because I didn't put in the effort to figure out the ambiguity around Noah/Shem and Nahor/Terah). I suppose there's one other hiccup, depending on which particular version of the Bible you're using. Since we don't have an 'original' version of Genesis, we have to rely on copies of that version, most notably the Masoretic text and the Septuagint (though those aren't the only two). And those copies differ on certain details, including all those ages in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11. Exodus to Solomon's Temple Like I said, this one comes straight from a single verse, 1 Kings 6:1: In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the Lord. Solomon's Temple to the Babylonian Captivity This is the period where things purportedly get a bit more complicated. I haven't gone through this period in detail, yet, myself, but to give just one example, you have this verse from 2 Kings 3:1: In the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria; he reigned twelve years. Go through finding all those verses and work out the years, and you come up a little over 4 centuries of history. In a somewhat independent path, other books in the Bible also give more genealogies, such that you can trace each and every claimed descendant from Adam all the way to Jesus. Granted, there aren't ages associated with all of those genealogies, but these also give a ballpark range in the thousands of years. So, if you accept the claims of the Bible at more or less face value, and assume all those genealogies represent real people and not just imaginary people made up out of thin air, and that all the events in Egypt, Israel, and Judah all really happened, you'll end up at an estimate for the date of creation somewhere around 4000 BC. As a side note, while it seems to be somewhat fashionable to dismiss exercises like these because some parts of the Bible were ‘obviously’ meant to be taken more metaphorically or allegorically, I don’t see such figurative interpretations as obvious at all. The crux of this argument would be the genealogies in Genesis 5 and Genesis 11 – after that, you’re already into Egyptian pharaohs, so nothing that’s going to be a major difference from real history (at least as far as timelines). But these genealogies aren’t fables with moral lessons or some type of simplified explanation of complex concepts for a pre-scientific society. They’re boring, dry lists of ancestry. It’s about as close to a conventional history section as you’ll find in Genesis – the part least likely to be metaphorical or allegorical (though there’s certainly a reason to ‘invent’ such lists to provide legitimacy for the rulers of Israel and Judah). *As I already touched upon, that difference of only a few decades is using a specific version of the Bible, such as the Masoretic text or the Septuagint. The differences between those different versions can add up to a couple millennia, though still not anywhere near on the magnitude of real history.

Should creationism be taught in public schools as an alternative to evolution, given its religious roots, or does doing so infringe upon the separation of church and state? There are two aspects of this answer. First, of course teaching creationism in public schools violates the separation of church and state in the U.S. This has repeatedly been the interpretation of courts, from Epperson v. Arkansas back in 1968 to the more recent Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District in 2005 (Ten Major Court Cases about Evolution and Creationism). But that's only a legal technicality. What if we didn't have the First Amendment, or lived in a different country that didn't enshrine the separation of church and state? Well, then we have the much more fundamental issue that creationism is wrong. I don't think many people realize that creationism was the dominant scientific paradigm prior to Darwin. Some naturalists may have toyed with ideas of 'transmutation', but they were largely seen as fringe eccentrics. At best, some naturalists were more in line with certain modern day creationists who concede evolution within 'kinds', but not universal common descent. It was the plausible theory and especially the evidence that Darwin presented in The Origin that basically convinced the scientific community practically overnight to accept evolution over creationism. In other words, those naturalists didn't reject creationism because they were a priori opposed to it, but because the evidence conclusively favored evolution over creationism. And in the 150+ years since then, the evidence for evolution has only grown even more overwhelming. So yes, teaching creationism in public schools in the U.S. would violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. But even more importantly, creationism is factually incorrect and not good science, so why would you want to teach it to our children in the first place?

Why do people say they believe science over God when science keeps changing what it says it’s proved and God has not changed? What do you mean that God hasn't changed? He's changed quite a bit over the millennia as the mythology developed. Since you're using capital-G for God, I assume you're referring to the God of the Bible, Yahweh (YHWH). While Yahweh's earliest origins are a bit obscure (and understandably so, since we're talking about something thousands of years ago), the leading idea seems to be the Midianite hypothesis, where Yahweh was originally a god worshipped by the peoples of Midian, the region to the south of Canaan. The early Israelites and Judahites, who were themselves basically just a subset of Canaanite culture at the time, absorbed this god into their pantheon while they still had a polytheistic pantheon. Of course, not all scholars agree with the Midianite hypothesis, and there are plenty of other origins ideas, including that Yahweh was more of a 'home grown' deity within Israel/Judah. On this topic of the earliest origins of Yahweh, the perhaps oldest known records of belief in this particular deity are a couple of inscriptions from Egypt – one from the period of Amenhotep III (14th century BCE), the other from Ramesses II (13th century BCE). In describing a certain group of people, both inscriptions use a phrase translated as something like "The Land of the Shasu yhw" or "Shasu of Yhw". Assuming that Yhw is the same god as YHWH, and that modern ideas of the Shasu being nomads of the region south of Canaan are correct, this seems to support the Midianite hypothesis for Yahweh's origins (though it should be noted, some people think the transfer went the other way around, with the Shasu adopting Yahweh from the Israelites). ABOVE: The inscription describing Shasu of Yhw SOURCE: Shasu - Wikipedia At any rate, no matter how Yahweh first entered the Israelite pantheon, his earliest appearances in Israelite religion were as just one god among many, and not even the most important. I've already discussed Deuteronomy 32:8–9 several times here on Quora, which clearly shows Yahweh as one of the sons of El, receiving Israel as his particular land to rule over, while other sons of El received different lands (more info: Jeff Lewis's answer to Can atheists prove there's no God, since they don't believe in His existence? in Divine Atheist). The earliest writings about Yahweh in the Bible also seem to present him as a storm god and god of war. The New Oxford Annotated Bible is an excellent resource, with very informative essays and copious footnotes from Biblical scholars. They mention this association with a storm god in several footnotes. For example, here was the footnote in reference to 2 Samuel 22:11–16: The LORD is depicted here as the storm God. Cherub (v. 11 ), a mythical, griffin‐like creature. God's voice (v. 14 ) is thunder (Job 40.9; Ps 29.3 ), and he throws lightning bolts at his enemies (v. 15 ). The psalmist envisions the world as flat; he is trapped in the underworld beneath the foundations of the world, which the LORD's roar uncovers (v. 16 ). Other footnotes made reference to "God's storm-cloud chariot" several places, including for Psalm 68:4 ("Who rides upon the clouds, God's storm‐cloud chariot (v. 33; Ps 65.11 )") and for Psalm 65:11 ("Your wagon tracks, God's rain‐cloud chariot."). Personally, reading the Bible on my own, I thought Psalm 77:16–20 was especially in line with those early conceptions of Yahweh as a storm god: When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; the very deep trembled. The clouds poured out water; the skies thundered; your arrows flashed on every side. The crash of your thunder was in the whirlwind; your lightnings lit up the world; the earth trembled and shook. Your way was through the sea, your path, through the mighty waters; yet your footprints were unseen. From those origins, Yahweh went through a transformation within the religion, gradually blending with El to become the primary and most important God of Israel, then through a stage where he was the only God that the Israelites were supposed to worship, though not yet the only god in existence, before the eventual transformation to full monotheism some time around the Babylonian exile. I have another answer where I discussed archaeological finds from during this transition which covers these next two examples in much more detail (Jeff Lewis's answer to Atheists, what are your top 5 reasons for not believing in God and/or Christianity? Please answer with something besides "No proof". in Atheism Now). First is the Mesha Stele, which recounts the same battle as told in 2 Kings 3, but from the point of view of King Mesha of Moab, and is actually older than the Biblical narrative. This stele shows how the Israelites were likely still worshipping more than one god ("the fire-hearth of Daudoh"), and that even their worship of Yahweh hadn't yet been centralized to the Temple of Jerusalem, contradicting the Biblical narrative. The second is the Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions, showing that Yahweh had a wife or consort at the time, the goddess Asherat. And like the Mesha stele, these inscriptions also contradict the Biblical narrative of a centralized worship at the Temple of Jerusalem. And of course, the character of Yahweh continued to develop and change over the generations, including the rise of Rabbinic Judaism after the destruction of the Second Temple, Christianity and it's updates in their scriptures, Islam and their updates, continued revisions in various sects over the years such as the Protestant-Catholic schism, and even more modern updates like Mormons and Jehovah's Witnesses. So in contrast to your implication, Yahweh has changed very much over the generations, from a storm god within a polytheistic pantheon, to the multiple conflicting conceptions of God among modern day Jews, Christians, and Muslims, and all the varying sects within those major branches. God seems to bear all the hallmarks of a mythological character who develops along with the culture of those folks who believe in him. As to the other part of your question, trust in science hardly even deserves a detailed explanation. But just to completely answer your question, here's an excerpt from my self-published book on religion (God? Leaving Christianity | jefflewis.net): One reason to be confident in the scientific process is pragmatic – just look at the results. Science as the formalized discipline that we think of has only been around a few hundred years, getting started in the Renaissance, but not really coming into its own until after the Enlightenment. And look at how fast our technology has progressed in that short time compared to the previous millennia of human existence. We’ve invented telescopes, steam engines, automobiles, semiconductors, airplanes, computers, TVs, radio, lasers, vaccines, antibiotics, cures for some cancers. We’ve sent people to the moon. These accomplishments are all based on knowledge that we’ve learned through science. We wouldn’t have been able to accomplish all of that if we didn’t have an accurate understanding of reality. Granted, there are other fields of science that haven’t yielded practical applications, and possibly never will. The Big Bang may not ever give us any new technologies. But given the technologies we have developed from so many other fields, we know that the methods produce reliable results.

How can I actually eat good to lose fat and get muscle? Because what I eat is a lot of both healthy and unhealthy. Like I might have some furit and eggs then like a pizza. Or have a salad then chip. How do I not overindulge and actually lose weight? I was about to write a long answer about how I managed this for myself, but then I noticed from other questions on your profile that you're only 13 years old, and that you've written many questions along these lines. So my advice at this stage in your life is to talk to your doctor at your next checkup and ask them about your weight and physique, rather than asking for advice from strangers on the Internet. The Internet is full of dangerous health advice along with the good health advice, and it can be difficult even for adults with years of experience to figure out which is which. And I don't mean this to be condescending, but as a 13 year old, still in the midst of school and with limited life experience, navigating this topic is going to be even more difficult for you, not to mention all the different considerations of development you're going through right now that adults no longer have to worry about. So talk to your doctor. They have the knowledge and expertise to give you good advice.

What percents of people do and don’t support abortion? Support varies by trimester. Here are the results of an AP-NORC poll from 2021: SOURCE: AP-NORC poll: Most say restrict abortion after 1st trimester In the first trimester, 61% of folks in the U.S. support keeping abortion legal in all or most cases, while only 38% want to see it illegal in all or most cases. However, as the pregnancy progresses, support for the legality of abortion drops. In the second trimester, only 34% of people want to see abortion remain legal in all or most cases. While in the third trimester, a mere 19% want the same thing.

Can a Republican ever win the presidency again without some kind of a reset? Anyone remember headlines like these from 2008, when Obama had a strong victory and Democrats won a majority in the House and a supermajority in the Senate? Well, it only took until 2010 for the Republicans to win back control of the House, which they held onto for 8 more years until the 2018 election. And while Obama did manage to win re-election in 2012, I think we all remember what happened in 2016. And even in 2020, Trump only lost thanks to about 40 thousand voters in 3 key swing states. Even this year, 538 is currently giving Trump a 40% chance of winning the election, which is barely worse than a coin toss. That's just the nature of our two party system and polarized politics. The Democratic and Republican candidates will always get roughly half the vote. And with the way the electoral college currently biases the results towards rural states that tend to favor Republicans, presidential elections in particular will remain competitive, even when Democrats might have a nationwide advantage in raw numbers. So yes, the Republicans still have a very good chance of winning the presidency even maintaining their current strategies. They have a very good chance of winning this year. So don't get complacent like 2016, thinking a Democratic victory is a sure thing. Everybody needs to get out and vote to make sure their voice is heard.

How would one "test God" (which is forbidden by The Bible's Deuteronomy 6:16)? Well, I think the Bible has already set the precedent for us in 1 Kings 18: 21 Elijah then came near to all the people and said, “How long will you go limping with two different opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him, but if Baal, then follow him.” The people did not answer him a word. 22 Then Elijah said to the people, “I, even I only, am left a prophet of the Lord, but Baal’s prophets number four hundred fifty. 23 Let two bulls be given to us; let them choose one bull for themselves, cut it in pieces, and lay it on the wood but put no fire to it; I will prepare the other bull and lay it on the wood but put no fire to it. 24 Then you call on the name of your god, and I will call on the name of the Lord; the god who answers by fire is indeed God.” And of course, when the prophets of Baal tried praying to their god, nothing happened. Then it was Elijah's turn to pray to his god, Yawheh. Elijah even showed off a bit by soaking his wood pile with water before praying. And then… 38 Then the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust and even licked up the water that was in the trench. 39 When all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, “The Lord indeed is God; the Lord indeed is God.” You can probably leave the steaks out of it. But just replicate Elijah's demonstration. God seemed perfectly willing and content to demonstrate his power a few thousand years ago. Why would he all of a sudden turn shy, now? Heck, he even performed this miracle in front of a bunch of skeptics, so it couldn't be anything about only revealing himself to people who were already believers and already had faith. Unless, of course, it's easy to tell tall tales about ancient history that can no longer be fact checked, but you need some excuse like Deuteronomy 6:16 to explain why these tall tales never seem to happen today*. *And yes, even back in Biblical times, they had their rose colored glass for their ‘good old days’, just like we do now. Remember, ‘Biblical times’ covers centuries. The oldest stories would have seemed ancient even to the folks living in the later periods of ‘Biblical times’. So Deuteronomy 6:16 was a convenient excuse even back then.

Why would anyone buy a hamburger at McDonald's when there are other hamburger places with better quality hamburgers at the same or lower prices? I challenge your premise. Let's go with prices, first. Here are the prices of fast food cheeseburgers at the fast food places I go to most often for burgers*, in my order of preference. I listed the bacon cheeseburgers at the other places, because while I get a plain cheeseburger at McDonald's, I usually go for the bacon cheeseburger at the other places (with the McDonald's cheeseburger being so minimalist with toppings, the salt in the patty and pickles is plenty, whereas the other burgers need the bacon to balance the lettuce and tomato). McDonald's has by far the cheapest cheeseburger. Granted, it's also the smallest. But it's still plenty of calories for a normal lunch. And if I'm extra hungry, I can get two, and it would still be cheaper than the other options. As far as flavor, McDonald's is my favorite out of the fast food places. There's just something about the McDonald's burger that hits just right, the perfect combination of those minimalist ingredients. I've said this before, but the other fast food places are trying to be like something I'd make on the backyard grill, and often not quite succeeding, while McDonald's is just doing its own thing. If I'm in the mood for a bunch of toppings, I might go to one of those other places (Whataburger is great at 2 am). But when I'm in the mood for a McDonald's cheeseburger, nothing else really matches it. If I've got a bit more time to sit down instead of going through a drive through, then I've got more options besides fast food. A local place called Pat's Drive In is probably my favorite restaurant burger in town ($4.79 for a cheeseburger), followed by a very small chain, Bricktown Brewery ($10.50 for a burger, but fries are included – and I can get a beer to go with it). So, out of fast food places, McDonald's does have my favorite burger, and it's the cheapest, to boot. It makes it the obvious choice when I'm in the mood for a fast food burger. *When I go to other fast food places, I tend to get chicken sandwiches, not burgers. e.g. Jack in the Box, Wendy's, etc. And since I live in a small town, we don't have some of the other national chains (though I've found a few of those to be overrated when I have tried them while traveling, e.g. In-n-Out – their burgers are fine, but their fries kinda suck). I guess I'll also briefly mention the fast-casual burger joint, Five Guys (not that there are any local after ours shut down, but looking down at the DFW area). They are pretty good, but damn are they expensive. A bacon cheeseburger is $12.69. Add a small fries and a drink, and the whole meal is up to $22.81. If I went to Bricktown Brewery, for that price I'd get a couple beers to go with my burger and fries. Five Guys is good, but it ain't that good.

What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary? First off, this question hits one of my pet peeves – using the word 'necessary' without any context, implying that 'necessary' is some intrinsic property all on its own. It isn't. Just about every time this word is used, it's in relation to a specific outcome. For example, are fermentable sugar and yeast necessary ingredients? Yes if you're making beer or bread. Not so much if you're grilling a steak. Considering that TV itself isn't a necessity, hardly anything around the medium is necessary in any universal sense. It all depends on what outcomes you want. So, if you're asking if these disclaimers are necessary – necessary for what? If you wanted to be cynical, you could say that the purpose of these disclaimers is merely a way to silence the busybodies with a token message that only lasts a few seconds, that most viewers will forget about almost as soon as the action starts. The network can still show controversial or 'problematic' content essentially unaltered, retaining most of the audience that enjoys those shows (and their associated advertising dollars). The networks have balanced the conflicting influences of alienating more politically correct viewers to losing more old fashioned viewers, and figured these disclaimers were the best compromise. It's the free market at work. If you want to be more charitable about their motivations, such disclaimers do play at least a small part in consciousness raising. It may only be a short message, but at least it's putting it in people's heads that these depictions may not be so benign. And so when they do watch these shows, they're not just uncritically accepting such depictions as right or normal. I think this is especially true when it comes to kids watching TV. I know, some folks like to say that parents should be aware of all the media their children are consuming. That's a bit unrealistic, not to mention a bit questionable advice in its own right. Such constant supervision has taken on its own derogatory term these days – helicopter parenting. On the other extreme, you have folks fondly remembering the 'good old days', when kids roamed their neighborhoods unsupervised for hours on end (and believe me, even back then, we found parents' stashes of 'questionable' media hidden in boxes in the attic). Ideal parenting is somewhere in between – a balance of oversight and child independence, where parents have a general idea of what their kids are up to, but not necessarily screening each and every TV show their kids are going to watch. And in this context, such disclaimers are important in the consciousness raising of children, who don't have the background and experience to fully understand such shows like adults. So yes. I think these disclaimers serve a purpose. They help in the consciousness raising of both nostalgic older viewers and younger first time viewers. And considering that it's such a short message and that the shows themselves are unaltered, it seems that it's only the most easily offended who get worked up about these disclaimers, anyway.

If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? In American English, 'burger' on its own most certainly refers to a ground beef patty on a bun. You can stretch the definition a bit by adding a description of some other ingredient besides beef, such as a chicken burger or a veggie burger, but the implication is that it's still a ground food of some sort formed into a patty. For example, this is a chicken burger. Note the ground chicken formed into a patty: ABOVE SOURCE: Natasha's Chicken Burgers While this, since it contains a whole piece of chicken that's been breaded and fried, is a chicken sandwich: ABOVE SOURCE: The OG Chick-Fil-A Sandwich Where you can run into a bit of a gray area is a ground beef patty that's not on a bun. If you put the patty in between two slices of grilled bread with cheese, then it's a patty melt. And then it's just a question of semantics as to whether or not you think a patty melt is a type of burger or something separate. The article I copied that image from does refer to it as a specific type of burger, and I tend to agree since the defining feature of a hamburger (with it’s origins from a Hamburg steak) is the ground beef patty. ABOVE SOURCE: This Is Why Whataburger Patty Melts Are So Delicious - Mashed Yes, I know that in some other countries, practically anything on a bun is referred to as a burger. I was a bit surprised (and relieved) one time going to a get together with my German friends, when they said they were going to make chicken burgers, but they were actually making what I would call chicken sandwiches. So to answer your question, in American English, the boundary between a burger and other sandwiches is using a ground meat (or veggie) patty. No patty – no burger.

For those who experienced the eclipse today, what are your thoughts? I've seen a few sources overhyping eclipses a bit, so I don't want to oversell it, but it was very, very cool. Living about 2 hrs outside the path of totality myself, it was definitely worth the trip to get myself into a location to see the total eclipse, since a total solar eclipse really is an altogether different experience than a partial solar eclipse. Since my wife is working a contract away from home right now and got a few days off, we decided to make an event of it. We both arrived in Ft. Worth the day before, and spent the day going to a small wine tasting festival and then a night out in downtown Ft. Worth (hat tip to The Flying Saucer). The next morning, the day of the eclipse, we drove down to Mansfield, a small town on the outskirts of the DFW metro area, since that's where most of my wife's family lives. There's nothing like last minute planning, so an hour before the eclipse was forecast to start, we were at Walmart buying hotdogs, hamburgers, and other supplies for a cookout, while my sister in law was scrambling to clean up her house. I did plan enough ahead to have my telescope ready to go, along with a sun funnel that I threw together on Saturday. I got that set up in her driveway as family members began rolling in, so we were able to track the eclipse with that, while everybody had their own eclipse glasses, too. Our eclipse watching group included a few of us who had the day off, one person who called in to take the day off, and a few nieces and nephews skipping the school day (worth it). ABOVE: The start of the eclipse through my telescope – note that this setup lets you see the sunspots, which you don't notice through eclipse glasses. Our biggest stressor was the weather. The forecast was for a cloudy day, and the day of did turn out to be partly cloudy. Throughout the time that the eclipse was occurring, we'd have clouds periodically roll in and block our view. There was one particularly big one that rolled into place as totality was getting close. Google told me that totality was supposed to start at 1:39 in Dallas, and I don't think that cloud blew out of the way until 1:36. So it cleared out just in time. Though I do feel sorry for the people downwind of us who had that cloud blow in just in time to block their view. When the sun was completely blocked by the moon, it really was awesome. I haven't seen many photos that do justice to what it looks like with your own eyes. This photo below is about as close as I've seen, though it was from a previous eclipse back in 2010. Per the description at the site where I found this, it's a composite image composed of short, medium, and long exposures. Compared to yesterday's eclipse, the below photo is missing a couple solar flares that we could just barely see as red spots along the edge of the moon. But this photo does give a sense of the wispy arms of the corona stretching out from the Sun. ABOVE CREDIT: Dennis Di Cicco ABOVE SOURCE: Basic Solar Eclipse Info — Great American Eclipse You've probably seen umpteen million descriptions of eclipses by now, but yes, it really did get dark and noticeably cooler during totality (it actually started cooling down before the Sun was completely blocked). It wasn't quite as dark as night, but more like the mid stages of dusk and dawn. We could make out a couple planets (Venus and Jupiter, I think), though not really any stars. We didn't have a great view of the horizon, and we were all focused on the eclipse itself, anyway, so I didn't notice the 360° sunset that others have mentioned. And I didn't notice any animals doing anything strange, either (though a flock of birds did fly overhead right as totality happened, which was pretty cool). One thing that seems obvious in hindsight is that I should have used sunscreen. Even partially blocked by the moon, staring at the Sun for a couple hours is still a lot of sunlight. A few of us ended up with a bit of a sunburn. Now, to address the overhyping, I've heard some people describe the eclipse as an almost spiritual or transcendent experience. Even Randall Munroe of XKCD fame said "A total eclipse is like someone broke the sky." Yeah, that's going too far. It's a very cool thing to see, but it's not life changing. If there's going to be an eclipse reasonably close by, or if you've got enough money to travel, it's worth seeing a total eclipse at least once in your life. I'd already seen multiple partial eclipses (including an annular eclipse just last year), and they simply don't compare to a total eclipse. But keep your expectations grounded in the fact that all it really means is that you're in a big shadow. A shadow cast by the Moon, but still just a shadow. ETA: I nearly forgot to mention, we also had an assortment of appropriately themed snacks. I had a hard time finding the Moon Pies, so I suspect we were far from the only people who did this.

Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how? People have been 'redesigning' life since the advent of domestication and selective breeding of crops and livestock. The big difference between that and intentional genetic engineering is that the old methods were haphazard, relying on willy nilly random mutations that nobody understood at all. It wasn't even until the last century or so that people even knew about genetics. So in the past, if somebody wanted to know if a new strain of crop that improved yield was also safe to eat, the only recourse was to eat enough of it to see what happened. Nowadays, we have enough of an understanding of the underlying genetics to already have an a priori idea of whether certain genetic changes will be safe or not. And we have more rigorous testing protocols for genetically engineered crops. Do I think such intentional genetic engineering can make life better? It certainly has the potential to do so. Take golden rice, for example. This is a new strain of rice engineering to have beta-carotene, a precursor to vitamin A, which can help drastically reduce Vitamin A deficiency in certain regions of the world where malnutrition is a problem. Or take Bt crops, so named for incorporating genes from the Bacillus thuringiensis bacteria, making proteins that are toxic to insects. This allows farmers to reduce the amount of insecticides they spray on their crops, with a secondary effect of reducing the greenhouse gas emissions from the equipment that does the spraying (FWIW, organic famers often spray a solution with the live bacteria onto their crops, since bacteria are 'organic'). ABOVE: A conventional rice variety on left compared to the more nutritious golden rice on right SOURCE: GM golden rice gets landmark safety approval in the Philippines So yes, genetic engineering is redesigning life, just like we’ve done for millennia, but in a much more controlled and less haphazard manner than traditional selective breeding. And yes, it certainly does have the potential to make life better. And if you were asking about the human genome, just ask anybody with a genetic disease if they'd like to be able to be cured. I lost a few childhood friends to cystic fibrosis. Genetic therapy would have been a literal life saver.

Do atheists believe Jesus was a person but no God? Yeah, sure. Probably. I know that there are a decent number of atheists who doubt that Jesus was a real person and think he was probably entirely legendary. But, while I don't think there's enough evidence to say anything conclusive, I do think it's more likely than not that he did exist. For one, it's a rather mundane claim. Charismatic leaders starting religious cults are a dime a dozen throughout history. We've got plenty in modern times and recent history, like Joseph Smith, L. Ron Hubbard, Jim Jones, David Koresh, Marshall Applewhite, Sun Myung Moon, Sathya Sai Babe, etc. Plenty even have stories of miracles they've performed. So the claim that a guy named Jesus (or the ancient equivalent of that name) founded a cult around 2000 years ago is not an extraordinary claim requiring extraordinary evidence. For another, unlike other mythical characters like Romulus and Remus, Robin Hood, or King Arthur, we've got Jesus pinpointed a lot more closely. Especially with the authentic letters of Paul, we've got a guy writing about this cult within living memory of Jesus, claiming to interact with folks who knew Jesus personally. We've also got the Gospels and a few extra-Biblical references from a few years later. And while the Gospels have plenty of problems around just how historically accurate they might be, it still seems reasonable that they'd be based on a real person, especially considering 'difficulties' that make more sense in light of trying to accommodate known details about a real person (the Nativity, Jesus's baptism, and the crucifixion itself). Sure, there's no eye witness or contemporary evidence, but how much of this type of evidence would you expect? If Jesus and his followers were illiterate peasants, they wouldn't have been writing much of anything themselves, so you wouldn't start to get things like Paul's letters or the Gospels until the popularity of the cult spread to more educated folks. And while some folks protest the lack of Roman records for things like the crucifixion, the fact is that we just don't have that many surviving records of anything like that from ancient Rome. Such records were written on perishable materials, so unless someone made an effort to save them, they didn't survive. We don't actually have records of any specific crucifixions from Rome, let alone Jesus's. So yeah. I think it's more likely than not that Jesus was a real cult leader 2000 years ago. As I already said, such cult leaders aren't exactly rare. The interesting thing about this cult is the way it struck a chord with so many people and rose in prominence. But that’s bound to happen from time to time, such as with later religions like Islam, Mormons, etc. For much more detail on the historicity of Jesus, here's one of the best answers I've ever come across on Quora. Note that some of the arguments for historicity also imply Jesus being an entirely human cult leader rather than divine:

Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life? The problem is that this literally isn't possible. The Bible contains many, many contradictions, so you simply can't verify and prove all of the stories. The best you can do is verify some of the stories. And at that point, we're left to cherry pick which stories and lessons we want to say are proven in this hypothetical scenario. Just to go with one example, are we going with the God of Exodus 20:5-6, who threatens "punishing children for the iniquity of parents to the third and the fourth generation," or the God of Ezekiel 18:19-20, who says that "A child shall not suffer for the iniquity of a parent nor a parent suffer for the iniquity of a child; the righteousness of the righteous shall be their own, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be their own"? Because the former seems quite barbaric and not at all worthy of worship. The latter at least seems fair. Still, though, the overall portrayal of God in the Bible is not particularly flattering. You've got the massacre of Noah's Flood with its drowning of infants and children, the horrific treatment of Egyptian commoners and their slaves in the Exodus story (Jeff Lewis's answer to Can you cite the verses of some morality flaws in the Bible?), and then the whole fiery furnace of Hell for the grave sin of doubt. And that's just scratching the surface. So, given all the contradictions within the Bible, even as a hypothetical, you can't imagine a scenario where all of it was proven true. But even going with the overall general portrayal of God in the Bible, he's not a being deserving of worship.

Does driving a manual transmission get annoying? It certainly can. Okak, let me establish my 'bona fides' before criticizing stick shifts. From high school through my first car after college, all I drove were stick shifts, including a year's worth of daily commuting in Washington, D.C. And that first car I bought for myself was a sports car, no less, because I really did enjoy driving for driving's sake. All that's to say that I was plenty comfortable and proficient driving a manual transmission. As so many people have said, under ideal conditions, you hardly notice the mechanics of shifting. It becomes second nature. There are even situations where it's especially handy, like choosing your gear on hills, push starting a car with a dead battery, or that time my brakes went out on me in a hand-me-down beater and I was able to nurse it home with downshifting and the emergency brake. But there are plenty of situations where stick shifts are decidedly less convenient. I injured my acromioclavicular (AC) joint in high school, and had to spend a few weeks with my arm in a sling. That would have been a non-issue with an automatic, but was a PITA with a stick. Then there are all the road trips where you swing through the drive thru to grab something to eat on the road – again, not ideal when you need one hand for shifting. My RX-7 made this problem even worse. In their quest to create a pure driver's experience, they didn't include cup holders. Running to Subway on your lunch break to grab something to take back to the office is a pain when you have to try to hold your drink while operating the clutch and gear shift. And while I got buy with a stick shift in D.C. rush hour traffic, my experiences later in life with automatics were definitely easier. When I got married, the vehicles we wanted for family vehicles tended to be available only as automatics. So, I've spent the last 20 or so years driving mostly automatic vehicles (minus an RX-8 that replaced my RX-7 as a more 'family friendly' sports car). And in all honesty, I don't miss the stick shift much at all. I thought I did, so I was excited when we got an automatic with paddle shifters that did give you control over exactly what gear you were in. But I only used those for about a week until the novelty wore off, and haven't really touched them since. As an engineer, I've also taken on a different mindset regarding manual transmissions. First off, they're a band-aid because of the crappy torque/power bands of internal combustion engines. Electric motors are showing that you don't need multi-speed transmissions if you have a better power source to begin with. Second, we engineers try to automate as much as practical to reduce the workload on operators. Early cars had manual timing advance, manual chokes, and all types of controls that just distracted the driver from their primary task of controlling the speed and path of the vehicle. The fact that stick shifts survived so long is not an endorsement of manual control of gear ratios, but a condemnation on us engineers that it took us so long to come up with better automatic transmissions. So yes, manual transmissions can get annoying. I'm not saying I'll never buy a stick shift again (I keep telling my wife that a 3rd gen RX-7 is going to be my midlife crisis car). But for my typical daily driver, I'll stick with automatics, and eventually something electric with a single speed gearbox that doesn't shift at all.

If atheism is true, why are there still monkeys? I thought monkeys evolved into humans over billions of years. The broad pattern of evolution is diversification to take advantage of new and varied ecological niches. Just for a moment, consider birds, and how many different species of birds there are today. You probably wouldn’t ask why other birds are still around if golden eagles evolved from birds. It hopefully seems obvious that golden eagles aren’t the only successful lifestyle for birds, and that there are lots of other ways for other bird species to survive without becoming more like golden eagles. In fact, it’s downright advantageous. There are only so many resources to go around in the golden eagle niche, so it’s better for other bird species to find other ways to make a living to have access to different resources. A hummingbird doesn’t have to compete with a golden eagle for food, while penguins can survive in environments that would kill eagles. It’s the same way with so many other branches of life, from beetles to ants to rodents to us monkeys. Successful lineages branch out and become more diverse, as they split up into more and more species to take advantage of more opportunities. Here’s a high level family tree of primates: ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982212008068 Now sure, you can play semantic games over whether those ‘Early simians’ should be called monkeys or not, but I think if we had a time machine and could bring one to the present, most people would think of it as a monkey. And monkeys have been a successful enough lineage that modern day monkeys have diversified into hundreds of species, from New World monkeys to Old World monkeys to apes, and yes, that includes us humans, as well. In other words, there are still other monkeys besides people because monkeys are a successful lineage, and there are lots of niches that they’ve evolved to take advantage of. Just to clarify, from those earliest monkeys to us humans has only taken tens of millions of years, not billions. And I know there are also more semantics around whether apes are monkeys or not, but I’ve come around to the idea that ‘monkey’ should be a monophyletic group, and that us apes should just be considered as a branch of monkeys.

What is the main ingredient in a sandwich? In many cases, there isn't a single main ingredient. All of the ingredients are important and work together in harmony. Take perhaps my favorite sandwich (and it's a fierce competition, since so many sandwiches are so damn good), the BLT. IMAGE SOURCE: BLT (Bacon, Lettuce and Tomato Sandwich) It's only five ingredients – the bacon, lettuce, and tomato that the name implies, plus toast and mayo. Screw up any single one of those ingredients, and your sandwich is hosed. And believe me, I've had hosed BLTs where restaurants tried to 'dress it up', only to ruin the balance. Things like using ciabatta instead of sliced bread, piling what seems like an entire pound of bacon onto a single sandwich, or using some trendy lettuce instead of a nice, crispy iceberg lettuce. You've got to get all of the ingredients right, and in the right balance, or the sandwich just isn't the same. Even something like a hoagie, which may seem like just piling ingredient on top of ingredient, still relies on getting all of the individual ingredients right. I once wrote an answer explaining how Subway sandwiches are only mediocre in comparison to real hoagies (Jeff Lewis's answer to Why don't people like Subway subs?), and posted this image for the comparison: Just at a glance, you can see the difference between the sterile excuse for a sandwich in the top left compared to the other three proper hoagies. And it’s not just one thing that makes the difference. Good hoagies need to get every single ingredient right, from the bread to the meats to the cheese to properly shaved onions. All of the ingredients are important. Good sandwiches don't have a single main ingredient. Every ingredient works together to make a sandwich what it is.

Why do creationists think the Earth is less than 4,000 years old? Because they take the Bible seriously. (Though as a slight correction, you got a bit mixed up on 4000 years old vs. the date of 4000 BC, which was actually around 6000 years ago: 4000 years BC + 2024 years AD). You can get a lot of the way there yourself looking at just two chapters of the Bible. Really, go take a look at these for yourself: These list genealogies from Adam all the way to Abraham, stating the ages when fathers had their sons. If you accept these genealogies, the Biblical account of creation, that Adam was the first person, and that Abraham was a real person who interacted with Egyptian pharaohs, then you've already got a good ballpark guess. I did a quick estimate myself. The only real ambiguity in those chapters comes in two places – the age of Noah when he had Shem, and the age of Terah when he had Abraham. But you're not looking at discrepancies that would be consistent with the Earth being 4.5 billion years old. After Noah was five hundred years old, Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. When Terah had lived seventy years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. So, for my estimate, I just used 500 and 70 for those two ages. I figure people who care about this issue more than me can dig deeper into getting better estimates. Here's what I came up with: So basically, 2000 years from the date of creation to the time of Egyptian pharaohs. If we go with the Middle Kingdom of Egypt, which was very roughly around 2000 BC, that puts the Biblical date of creation around 4000 BC. You can go further, looking at other books of the Bible, especially when all the various kings of Israel and Judah reigned and for how long, but that's a lot more digging to find all those individual verses. Of course, other folks have put in the effort. One of the most meticulous and rigorous, and for this reason also one of the most famous, was Archbishop James Ussher. Contrary to what a lot of people seem to imply, he wasn't the only scholar to do this, nor was he some eccentric outlier in thinking you could accept these Biblical sources as more or less reliable. His estimate just happened to be particularly well respected, so it's the one most remembered today. And going through all that detailed math, he came up with an estimate of 4004 BC. Of course, I hope it hardly needs to be said that modern science has shown this 'history' to be more than a bit off. But if you take the Bible seriously and at more or less face value, as plenty of people did for generations, you end up with an implied date for the creation of the world some time around 4000 BC. Full disclosure: It actually depends on which copy of the Bible you're using. Two of the major 'versions' are the Septuagint and the Masoretic Text, and they list different ages of the fathers throughout Genesis 5 and Genesis 11, resulting in around a 2000 year discrepancy. Still, they do have full genealogies from Adam to Abraham, so unless one of those guys lived to be 4 billion years old, they're still not in line with the actual age of the Earth.

If could put a space plane in a 100km high orbit, would the small amount of lift move it in to a higher orbit? Look at it this way. If you had a normal plane at a normal altitude and cut the engines, do you think the plane will start going higher because of the lift? No. Because airplanes also have drag, and that drag will rob the aircraft of energy. Without the thrust from the engines, the only way to maintain speed is to use gravity to descend. If a space plane were in orbit to where there was enough atmosphere to create a non-negligible amount of lift, it would also create a non-negligible amount of drag. That drag would begin to slow the space plane down. That in itself would be enough to make the plane begin losing altitude because of the way orbits work (you’re always falling, it’s just that your horizontal velocity keeps you moving sideways fast enough that you keep on ‘missing’ the ground). If you did want to maintain your speed without using engines, you’d have to descend even faster.

👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? I guess there are two shades of meaning to this question. Why did people write about Jesus at all (which I'll cover first). And why did so many people write about him in particular, to the relative exclusion of similar cult leaders at the time (which I'll get to a bit later). Broadly speaking, people were motivated to write about Jesus for the same reasons that they write about anybody. I've discussed a more modern day cult leader here on Quora before, Sathya Sai Baba*. He just died relatively recently in 2011, and you can find a ton of stuff written about him by his followers, from an official biography, to innumerable online essays by rank and file followers. You can even find answers by many of his followers right here on Quora (just type his name into the Quora search bar). Whatever you might think of his own motivations (e.g. were his 'miracles' intentional sleight of hand deception), he struck a chord with people and was able to parlay that into fame and a successful movement in his lifetime. Will Sai Baba's cult survive for centuries like Jesus's did? Who knows? Some sects seem to die out with the death of their leader, while others seem to resonate even afterwards. There are plenty of examples of this persistence, from major religions right down to smaller sects – Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Mormons, Seventh-day Adventists, Rastafarianism, Scientology, etc. I don't think there's really any way of knowing why Jesus's cult became so hugely popular compared to all the other similar cults in that time and place. Heck, history has relegated John the Baptist to basically supporting cast in the Jesus story, despite being a leader of a religious movement in his own right.** There have actually been studies on smaller scale versions of this. Back in 2003, some researchers created a music download website that they could control to run experiments. They tested a specific set of songs across multiple groups. None of the groups could see what songs the other groups had downloaded or how the other groups rated all of the songs. So in each group, there was equal opportunity for any song to go 'viral'. And what they found that was it was probabilistic and random at the same time (stochastic). Some songs tended to end up in the top downloads more often, while other songs tended to remain relegated to the bottom, but the specific songs that became the most popular varied from group to group with no way to definitively predict it ahead of time. It seemed to come down to random chance and extreme sensitivity to initial conditions. Here’s a pop-sci article discussing the study, and the actual research report: So, there probably was something to Jesus's message about loving your neighbor, caring for the poor, and not being judgmental that resonated with people. But why that particular cult ended up becoming a major world religion as opposed to the similar cults is probably down to chance. Had history played out a bit differently, billions of people might now be worshipping John the Baptist, wearing necklaces with dinner platters instead of crucifixes. * That previous answer about Sathya Sai Baba can be found here: ** It’s interested to read Josephus’s mention of John the Baptist, where he describes John the Baptist as an important figure in his own right, not some second fiddle to Jesus like in the Gospels:

The high level theory is known as the Modern Synthesis, or perhaps the Extended or Integrated Synthesis, depending on who you're talking to. This high level theory is itself composed of many other theories, laws, and principles, such as Gause’s Law, Bergmann's rule, or Dollo's law of irreversibility. Just like Newton's Laws, these laws within evolutionary theory are short, pithy statements or formulas to explain a concept, and not on the same broad explanatory level as an entire theory. ABOVE SOURCE: reddit So there you have it. Creationists have been claiming the imminent demise of science for nigh on two centuries, now, and I don't expect them to stop any time soon. They're the boy who cried wolf, but who then got their kids, grandkids, and great-grandkids to carry on crying wolf long after everyone else quit paying attention to them. And as far as evolution being a theory – of course it is. Theories are exactly the broad frameworks that get covered in science classes.

If you are an atheist, do you like Sam Harris? What about Richard Dawkins? Out of those two, I only ever paid much attention to Richard Dawkins, so I'll limit my comments to him. He's... okay. Back around 20 years ago when I first started on my path to atheism, Dawkins was one of the leading voices for atheism and science (not the same thing, but so-called 'New Atheism' did/does rely heavily on science). He seemed to be a pretty sensible guy. He was involved in some good public campaigns for atheism (e.g. the Atheist Bus Campaign), and some more questionable ones (e.g. the Brights movement). But by and large, he was a reasonable voice for godlessness. If he was a 'militant' atheist, then there wasn't that much actual militancy within atheism. I finally purchased and read The God Delusion after I was already an atheist (I was too ashamed to be seen buying it at my local bookstore when I was still struggling with religion). It was a decent book that introduced me to things I'd never thought of before, though I haven't gone back to read it recently to see how well it holds up. The next book of his that I read was The Greatest Show on Earth, devoted to explaining the evidence for evolution. But I felt like he spent too much of that book harping on creationism, rather than focusing on the far more interesting topic of evolution itself. I read two other books on evidence for evolution around that same time, Jerry Coyne's Why Evolution Is True, and Donald Prothero's Evolution: What the Fossils Say and Why it Matters, and I recommend both of those books head and shoulders above Dawkins' Greatest Show on Earth. They both found a much better balance of dealing with creationism without it becoming distracting. After that, I read The Magic of Reality. This one was marketed to readers of all ages as a sort of broad science lesson on several topics, from 'Who was the first person' to rainbows to earthquakes. But once again, he harped so much on religion that it felt a bit like The God Delusion for Kids. His axe to grind against religion caused him to miss an opportunity to focus on the science. After that, I'm not sure if I drifted away from following him as closely, or if he himself drifted out of the public eye, but I didn't pay as much attention to him in the following years. I did notice from time to time that he seemed to stick his foot in his mouth on Twitter (I'm honestly not sure if he's even still active on 'X'). But given his age and the way plenty of old people don't keep up with shifting societal norms, while that might be a tad disappointing, it's not shocking (I cringed plenty of times listening to my own older relatives complaining about the changing times). Anyway, I found Dawkins to be a useful voice for atheism and science a couple decades ago when I first became an atheist and when I got involved in the Skeptical movement. After that, I found that he allowed his obsession with religion to mar what could otherwise have been better books. And then after that, I just kind of drifted away from following him, so I can't say too much about his present day activities.

Democrats support post-birth abortion, but isn’t abortion after birth just murder? What I think is enlightening is the opinion of medical professionals who actually have to deal with such situations on a regular basis. Here's a study from just a few years ago: This poll "was conducted among all physicians and paramedical professionals involved in late TOP [termination of pregnancy] decision‐making in all eight centers with a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit in Flanders, Belgium (N = 117)". These aren't folks for whom this question is a mere hypothetical. They have to see the consequences and suffering of the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit on a daily basis. When posed with the statement, "For newborn children presenting a serious condition it is, in certain cases, acceptable to actively terminate life", a full 89.1% of all such health care professionals agreed, rising to 93.6% among the physicians. On a separate but related statement over methods, "Feticide is to be preferred to palliative care", majorities still favored the active approach – 57.8% of all health care professionals, 53.2% of the physicians. But extending a baby's life in certain serious cases isn't mercy or caring. It's only prolonging their suffering while delaying the inevitable. FWIW, most people in the general public, Democrats and Republicans, Pro-Choice and Anti-Choice, don't hold the same views as the medical professionals. The vast majority of the general public is opposed to late term abortions, and the idea of feticide is so taboo that you don't even find polls that ask about it.

Why are non-professional cyclists drawn to road bikes? Back when I was in college, I bought a somewhat decent mountain bike* to get around. I didn't give a whole lot of thought to mountain bike vs. road bike at the time. I mean, mountain bikes just sounded cooler, and it seemed that a mountain bike would be more robust to the abuse of daily riding, jumping curbs, hitting potholes, and the like. It was fine, got me to and from campus, and I even took it on a nearby trail a handful of times. Riding a bike daily like that for over 2 years got me pretty accustomed to cycling. Fast forward a few years to living in Wichita Falls, Texas, and we have a huge cycling event known as the Hotter'n Hell Hundred, so named for a 100 mile route in potentially 100°F weather (though it now takes place in the morning and so isn't usually quite that hot). A group of us decided to participate one year just to say we did it, but sticking with a shorter 25 mile route. One friend was really into cycling, so he offered to go down to a place in Dallas to pick up good road bike rentals for the weekend – bikes up in the several thousand dollar range if we were going to buy them. ABOVE: The Mass Start at the Hotter'n Hell Hundred SOURCE: 40th Hotter 'N Hell Hundred event photos When I first got up on that road bike and pressed down on the pedal... Wow! The bike just glided across the pavement like it was nothing. And when I stopped pedaling, the bike didn't stop. It just kept on coasting and coasting seemingly forever. There was just no comparison between that road bike and the mountain bike that I'd ridden back in college. The road bike was supremely optimized to be low friction for riding on pavement. Now, I'm still not sure a road bike would have been the best option for me in college with the amount I abused my bike. And there's no way I would have been able to shell out several thousands of dollars for a road bike comparable to that one I rented. But after riding a good road bike when all I was used to before was a mountain bike, I can definitely understand why people opt for road bikes. I mean, it’s in the name. That’s what they’re designed for. *My bike in college was a Raleigh M50 - looked just like this: 2000 Raleigh M50 Front Suspension Mountain Bike for Sale in Mechanicsburg, PA - OfferUp. If memory serves, it cost somewhere around $300 back in the 90s, which would be the equivalent of around $600 today. So not a world class bike, but definitely better than what you find in a typical Walmart.

How do atheists respond to the saying "everything happens for a reason" after experiencing something negative? Is there a counter argument from an atheist perspective? Why do we need a counter argument? You're the one with the saying with troubling implications for reality – that we're all at the mercy of some cosmic puppeteer putting us through the ringer for unfathomable reasons beyond our control. I mean, the common expression is to 'accept your fate', not 'embrace' it or 'rejoice in' it. There's a sense of resignation, of submitting to the biggest bully on the block. So I guess the simplest atheist 'counter argument' is that no, the universe isn't quite that bad. Bad things beyond our control may still happen, but at least it's not some entity toying with us on purpose. However, if you want some more common expressions, there are plenty. One of my favorites that I use quite often is, 'It is what it is.' If you want to sound a bit fancier using a foreign language, you could say 'Que será, será.' Or if you want to go a little more low brow, you can go with the old standby, 'Shit happens.' All of these have a similar intent behind them, that we live in a universe where many things will happen beyond our control. It does no good to dwell on why or what if*, because that still won't change it. Our best course of action is to accept those things, and then do the only thing we can do, control how we react and what actions we ourselves take going forward. *Of course, I don't mean to ignore causes altogether if understanding those causes can help inform your actions in the future. I mean 'why' and 'what if' in a more metaphysical sense. For example, understanding the causes of an airplane accident can drive regulations, retrofits, or training to avoid future accidents. But there's nothing we can do to change accidents that have already happened.

If someone was hypothetically able to view the light that left Earth 65 million years ago during the Cretaceous period, what would they see and witness? I assume you picked 65 million years hoping to see dinosaurs. But in reality, you’re going to see something like this: ABOVE SOURCE: Jwst Feed (@jwstfeed.bsky.social) Yes, that’s an entire galaxy, not a single solar system, let alone a single planet like Earth. That is the galaxy known as NGC 3972, which is around 60–65 million light years away. This image was captured with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which is one of the most powerful telescopes ever built. Here’s another photo of the same galaxy by another incredibly powerful telescope, Hubble: ABOVE SOURCE: NGC 3972 - Wikipedia The issue is that 65 million light years is a long way away. The other issue is that telescopes can only ‘magnify’ an image so much. Because of the wave nature of light, as opposed to being pure rays, there’s essentially a limit to how much you can focus the image depending on how big your mirror is. That in turn limits how much detail you can make out. It’s not an issue of cramming a higher resolution scanner into your telescope. That would just give you a higher resolution of an out of focus image. I’ve gone through the math before in other answers. But if you wanted to make out a triceratops to roughly the resolution shown below from 65 million light years away, you would need a telescope 260 light years in diameter. That’s not gonna happen. Even solar gravitational lens telescope proposals only increase the effective diameter to that of a star, which is still well short of 260 light years. (That’s Galileo in the bottom right for scale, by the way.) The other issue that people tend not to think about is exposure times. If you look up the image info for NGC 3972 at HubbleSite.org, it lists exposure dates from April - July, 2015. Now, I’m not sure if it was focused on that single galaxy for the entire time. But still, you’re looking at a long exposure time to generate such an image. So if you were hoping to see individual dinosaurs, they’re not going to sit still that long for a portrait. Basically, with any type of realistic telescope technology, the best your going to do is a nice picture of the Milky Way galaxy. Maybe you’ll be able to pick out the Sun, but trying to image Earth on it’s own, let alone in any detail to see individual animals, just ain’t gonna happen. Related answers:

Evolutionists have been debating the chicken and chicken egg question for a long time. Can evolution explain which came first? No, because evolution helps us to understand that it's not the type of thing you can pinpoint. It would be like trying to define the precise second when dusk becomes night, or the precise date that a child becomes an adult. It just doesn't work that way. These are gradual processes that elude precise demarcations. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. In sexually reproducing animals, there's no single individual that's a different species from their parents, or indeed, the entire population of which they're a part. Plus, there's plenty of genetic variability within a population, which will be recombined in all types of different ways as the animals mate. So you can't even pick an individual organism as the first chicken, after which all of its descendants will subsequently be chickens, as that individual and its descendants will still have to mate with other members of the population, continuing to mix up those genes.
