Why are there still altruists evolutionarily? I hate to say it, but the other answers to this question, even from folks who normally write good stuff, are wrong, misleading, or fudging the definition of altruism. True altruism goes beyond mere cooperation or being helpful. It means being helpful without any benefit to yourself, or from an evolutionary perspective, at least a benefit to your own genes. And natural selection is never going to favor such behaviors of pure altruism. To the extent that altruism does happen and has an evolutionary origin, it's because evolution is a mindless process without perfect aim, and some behaviors are missing their target. To begin with, there's the concept of kin selection. What's really important to evolution is increasing the copies of your genes. When parents help their direct offspring, nobody refers to that as 'altruism', since the offspring share half of the genes from each parent, so it's obvious that the parents are protecting their own genetic legacy. But you share genes with more relatives than just your own children. As the famed biologist JBS Haldane supposedly once quipped, "I would gladly give up my life for two brothers or eight cousins." Promoting your own genes by helping relatives is not altruism, at least in an evolutionary sense. Cooperation beyond relatives can also be favored by natural selection, but that's because cooperation brings benefits to all parties involved, so it's not really altruism, either. This can even cross species boundaries, such as the textbook example of cleaning stations in coral reefs, where cleaner fish and shrimp will pick the dead skin and parasites off of larger fish, even fish that could easily eat them if they tried. The cleaners get a meal, while the cleanees get improved hygiene. Everyone benefits from this cooperation (well, everyone but the parasites). One of the other answers to this question used the example of helping an injured member of your tribe to recover, so that they can once again become productive and contribute to your tribe in the future. Well, that's the ulterior motive right there – their future contributions. Going even further, in complex social groups like we humans form, individuals benefit immensely from being a part of the tribe, but everybody also has a vested interest in keeping out freeloaders and cheats. So public displays of charity help to increase your social capital, showing that you are a valuable, contributing member of the tribe, which will provide you with indirect benefits down the road. So even public displays of charity aren't altruistic in these conditions. (I’m not saying people are so conniving in their motivations, but why evolution would have instilled such instincts in us.) The tribalism that's so common in human societies helps to show that these behaviors really are for the benefit of the individual, and not altruism. From a selfish perspective, it makes sense to help out those in your own tribe, since they're more likely to be family in the first place (kin selection), or folks who will be able to help you out in the future (long term cooperation). People are much, much less charitable to non-relatives, or to those outside their own tribe (the other). But like I said way up in the beginning, evolution doesn't have perfect aim. It's not a conscious creator who implements designs the same way an intelligent designer might. Evolution often results in good enough, not perfection. So a general instinct to help those in your own tribe will be helpful, but could spill over into helping strangers. Parental instincts to help your own children and those of your near relatives can spill over into helping babies in general. And of course, in the more intelligent animals like us apes, dolphins & whales, some birds, and a few others, our extremely complex personalities provide even more opportunities for individuals to consciously choose actions that may not be in their evolutionary best interests. It doesn't mean natural selection favors those choices, but rather that natural selection does favor the larger set of complex behaviors, because their benefits outweigh the occasional 'poor' choice (poor in an evolutionary sense, not necessarily in a moral one). Finding examples of true altruism that weren't just the occasional misfiring of otherwise evolutionarily beneficial behaviors would actually be a major blow to our current understanding of evolution. Outside the somewhat controversial theories of group selection, there's no mechanism to explain why an organism would help out another organism if it didn't gain at least some benefit for itself or its genes. But cooperation, tit-for-tat, kin selection, and complex behaviors in intelligent animals do all go to show that the alternative isn’t a cut-throat, dog eat dog world. There are still plenty of reasons evolution will favor cooperation, since cooperation can bring benefits to everybody.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I've met intelligent creationists, but never any creationists in person who actually understood evolution. Every time I talked to an intelligent creationist about how they thought evolution worked, I invariably found that they didn't actually understand. Their views tend to be a mish-mash of Lamarckism, teleological thinking, evolution being progression towards a goal, and human exceptionalism, along with a lack of knowledge of how evolution works, and even a lack of knowledge of modern day organisms. These types of misconceptions drive such questions as wondering why there are still monkeys if we evolved from monkeys (though it's never why there are still birds if penguins evolved from birds), or wondering whether the first fish to crawl onto land would have had either gills or lungs (totally ignoring all the existing fish that have both). You can browse through the Index to Creationist Claims to get an idea of the types of arguments creationists might use. I don't wholly blame these folks, either. They were raised in an environment where creationism was the default, from their parents to their preachers, to possibly even their school teachers (my daughter's high school biology teacher made an announcement at the start of the lesson on evolution that, as a Christian, she didn't believe in it, herself, but it was just part of the curriculum that they had to get through). They were taught all these misleading creationist arguments from people they trusted from a very young age. So the smartest kids were actually the best at absorbing those lessons. And since it takes a while for people to fully develop critical thinking skills, and a fair amount of discipline to go back and apply that to things you think you already know, it's hardly a surprise that those bright kids brought up within a creationist environment carried that belief into their adulthood. (And to be fair, ask yourself how you know that matter is composed of atoms and that atoms are composed of even smaller particles – do you really understand the evidence, or is it just common knowledge that you were taught back when you were younger?) I will say, though, that the number of intelligent, well-educated creationists I've met is rather small. You can definitely see a correlation vs. education level (note that graph is a bit old from 2005): SOURCE: Americans Weigh In on Evolution vs. Creationism in Schools So yes, I've met otherwise intelligent folks who were also creationists. But once you talk with them, it almost invariably turns out that, for whatever reason, they don't actually understand evolution. I have yet to meet a single person in real life who could accurately explain evolution yet still rejected it.

If a ball is spinning and generating artificial gravity, would the force be on the outer surface or inner surface? A ball is not really a great shape for this. When engineers talk about spinning a spaceship or space station to create artificial gravity, what it really is is centrifugal force. I'm not going to get into a big discussion on centripetal vs. centrifugal force. Just realize that in a rotating reference frame, centrifugal force is a 'useful fiction' to help engineers calculate forces while keeping their coordinate system aligned with the rotating object, and that centripetal force points towards the axis of rotation. ABOVE: Centripetal force is the 'real' force in a non-rotating reference frame. Centrifugal force is the useful fiction from the rock's point of view. SOURCE: Centrifugal Force- Definition, Principle, Examples (vs Centripetal force) For this reason, when engineers propose rotating space ships or space stations to create 'artificial gravity', they tend to follow a few standard forms that make the best use of centrifugal force. The simplest is putting your main crew compartment and some type of counterweight on opposite ends of a tether, and having them spin around their common center of gravity, with the tether holding them together. ABOVE SOURCE: Should we give up on artificial gravity? A common one in sci-fi stories for a bigger ship/station is to make it into a ring, so that you can take advantage of the entire ring for artificial gravity. Here's the classic example from 2001: A Space Odyssey: SOURCE: Sci-fi Gifs And here's kind of what it would be like inside such a station: SOURCE: Quora For the really fanciful sci-fi stories, they might use something know as an O'Neill cylinder. This is a truly gigantic version, where you have a huge cylinder spinning, which can create entire enclosed habitats: ABOVE: I know the labels are in Russian (I can't read them, either), but it's about the best diagram I could find SOURCE: Humanoid History (@HumanoidHistory) on X That said, there are some very significant engineering challenges to doing any of these configurations, such that none of them may be practical, especially in the near term. For any upcoming missions to Mars, for example, the astronauts are probably just going to have to deal with a zero-g journey. So, with all that explanation, I hope the answer to your question is obvious. The artificial gravity will be on the inside surface of your spinning ball, due to the centrifugal force 'pushing' you away from the axis of rotation. If you were on the outside surface, you would be flung away from the ship/station. But you should also see why a ball wouldn't be a great shape for this. Only the 'equator' would have the centrifugal force perpendicular to its surface. Everywhere else would be on a slope, like a hill. The points right at the axis of rotation would be completely vertical from an astronaut's perspective.

Why is there so much debate over the math question 12÷2(2+4) =? A few other answers have said it's because the expression is ambiguous. But that's not really it. The expression isn't ambiguous at all. As an engineer myself, there's only one way to interpret that expression correctly. No. The issue is that lots of folks' exposure to math doesn't go much if at all beyond the high school level, and simplistic understandings of order of operations like PEMDAS or BODMAS. They don't know any further conventions that affect order of operations. The thing that makes this expression completely unambiguous is that there's no symbol in between the 2 and the parenthesis. That makes it clear that 2(2+4) is a single unit that can't be broken up. So the only appropriate way to interpret this expression is: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) What might have made this expression a bit ambiguous would have been to add a multiplication symbol: 12÷2×(2+4) Then it could be conceivable to interpret it a bit differently, perhaps instead as: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) However, even then, many engineers might interpret it the first way, keeping 2×(2+4) as a single unit as the denominator of the fraction. The reason is that when you're writing math 'inline' as opposed to formatting it the way math should really be written, division symbols are often treated as the fraction bar, with everything to the left assumed to be the numerator, and everything to the right assumed to be the denominator, and not cluttering things up with parentheses. As just one example, here are the definitions of some coefficients from one of my own engineering books, which I can assure you follow the convention that I just described (“my own” is in I own it, not that I wrote it). Really, if you wanted it to be 12/2, you'd probably put the parentheses around that to make it clear that 12/2 was a fraction, and instead write something like: (12/2)(2+4) But just to summarize, the expression as written in the original question isn't ambiguous. The issue is that lots of folks with only limited exposure to math don't know all the conventions affecting order of operations. And if there ever are any questions about ambiguity in an expression you’re writing, don’t be afraid to use parentheses.

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? I don't see any 'holes', per se. It just doesn't seem practical for any real world purposes. If I understand the description in the question, you'll end up with something like this on your sub: You've got a tank big enough to allow 1 gallon of sea water to drive a turbine to generate power, and that power will be used for electrolysis to create hydrogen and oxygen. Pressure can be thought of as energy per volume: So, just rearranging a bit, energy is pressure times volume. You need some type of pressure differential to get any work out of that, which is why the contraption has that tank at atmospheric pressure in the diagram above. But since atmosphere pressure is so much lower than the water pressure that deep, we can just assume it's negligible. Anyway, assuming everything was 100% efficient (which it won't be), using the correct value of 16k psi for the pressure in the deepest part of the ocean, and that I’ve done all my math properly, that 1 gallon of water has a potential energy of 308k ft-lb or 0.156 hp-hr, or in terms more familiar to folks who aren't U.S. based engineers, 418 kJ or 116 Wh. In contrast, a AA battery has roughly 3.9 Wh. So your device, at most, has the potential to generate as much energy as 30 AA batteries. In actuality, after all of the efficiencies are accounted for, it will be even less than that. I think your sub is going to need more than 30 AA batteries worth of energy to complete its mission, so you're spending more energy to perform this mission than what you get out of it. So, while this device could theoretically generate hydrogen in principle, there are far more practical ways of generating power.

I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true? You've got a weird way of approaching this question. Take fairies, for example. As you said, if you "can't make [your]self believe something without evidence", and there's no compelling evidence for the existence of fairies, the default position is to lack belief in fairies, or to take a non-fairiest worldview. If you needed some type of positive evidence for the non-existence of fairies, you'd be stuck in some weird ontological limbo. With no evidence for the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in fairies, but with no evidence against the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in their non-existence. But it's not just fairies. This goes for anything. You can build up positive evidence for the existence of something. It's much, much harder to build up evidence for the non-existence of something. That's why the burden of proof has developed the way it has. In general, it's up to the person claiming that something exists to prove their case. The rest of us have no need to take their claims seriously until they have such evidence. To borrow a somewhat silly example from the Internet, do you have any evidence against the existence of Eric The God-Eating Magic Penguin? Wouldn't it seem a bit ridiculous to say that just because you can't find any evidence against Eric, that you're not going to take the non-Ericist position? I hope you see where this is going. If gods exist, the burden of proof is on the people claiming that they exist. Until they can provide compelling evidence, the rest of us are under no obligation to take their claims seriously. Just like with fairies, the lack of evidence makes the default position a non-theistic worldview.

Marriage I remember when our Catholic priest found out my parents had been married in a Lutheran church. He said something to the effect of, 'You mean you're not married?' How is it possible for a specie to pass on evolved genes when it has no power to send genetic messages to its descendants billions of years down the line? I don’t expect anyone to know the answer to this one? You've correctly hit on a major misconception that many people seem to have about evolution – that certain mutations or traits should somehow appear in anticipation of some future adaptation. But as you pointed out, that can't happen. Just take a look at the natural world around us today. Every organism is adapted to its current environment and niche. All organisms throughout history have been the same way. The only mutations that were favored by natural selection were beneficial to those organisms in their own time and place. Where some creationists go off the rails is failing to see how certain adaptations could have been the result of countless intermediate stages. Perhaps the quintessential example is eye evolution. The common creationist argument is something along the lines of eyeballs being exquisitely interconnected systems that wouldn't function without all of their current components in place. As I've seen it put too many times, 'What use is half an eye?' But less complex eyes than our own really are useful and functional. We see them in living animals, from something like a hydra which has only photo-sensitive neurons, to starfish with pigment spots, to snails with pigment cups that can detect direction of light without making an image, to nautiluses with pinhole eyes without a lens, to complex 'camera' eyes like us humans or squids. ABOVE: Evolutionary pathway for camera eyes SOURCE: Visualizing the Evolution of Vision and the Eye ABOVE: And since not all eyes are like ours – Evolutionary pathway for compound eyes SOURCE: Visualizing the Evolution of Vision and the Eye Evolution didn't need to preserve adaptations towards a full camera eye in anticipation of that complex configuration. Every step along the way was a useful adaptation, improving the vision in each of those organisms. I've seen this question asked about plenty of other adaptations as well, from arms and legs, to the lungs of us land animals (many people don't seem to know how many existing fish breathe air), and more. I don't want to make this answer too long, but if you're curious about some of those other traits, here are a few more answers you might want to read: Anyway, I hope this answer helps. You're correct in that natural selection can't favor mutations in anticipation of some far off future benefit. Mutations have to be beneficial to an organism in its immediate surroundings. But over many generations, building incrementally on the benefits of generations past, this has still lead to remarkable adaptations.

Can a truck be engineered to fly by designing the gearing required to extract torque off the motor's axis and using it to move the right sized props? If it had retractable wings, would the engine be powerful enough to keep it in stable flight? Let's take a look at this with some simple back of the envelope math. Google tells me that an 18 wheeler weighs around 35,000 lbs empty, and around 80,000 lbs fully loaded, while they typically have around 500 hp engines. Here's a graph of peak lift to drag ratios (L/D) of various aircraft. Our 18 wheeler with retractable wings isn't going to be anywhere near as streamlined as any of these planes, but just for the sake of argument (remember, this is just a back of the envelope calculation), let's be optimistic and pick an L/D of 20. ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Variation-of-L-D-max-for-different-aircrafts_fig8_321107730 So, for the empty truck weighing 35,000 lbs, a L/D of 20 means it will have a drag of 1750 lbs, and hence need to create a thrust matching that. For the fully loaded 80,000 lb truck, that works out to 4000 lbs of drag/thrust. Next, we can just use the super simple fact that you can calculate power based on thrust and velocity as: P=T*V Or, going the other way around: T=P/V Keep in mind, this is ignoring other limitations based on the physical limitations of how propellers work and the resulting losses in real life, predicting impossibly high thrust values at low airspeeds. But it sets an absolute upper limit of thrust possible for a given power. And again, remember – back of the envelope. I already did all the proper unit conversion on a spreadsheet (e.g. hp to ft-lb/s, and mph to ft/s), so here's how that graph of max thrust vs. airspeed works out: So, if you could pull off an L/D of 20 at low airspeeds (which would be a feat in itself), you could conceivably just barely fly a 35,000 lb aircraft with a 500 hp engine, but it'd be pushing it. And you wouldn't be able to go much over 100 mph before you ran out of power. For the fully loaded 80,000 lb truck, forget it. You're simply not going to be able to generate enough thrust with that engine. If I took this analysis a step further, and actually did some simple modeling of propellers, looking at the thrust you could get for a given diameter, it would just get even worse. Momentum theory sets further limitations on propeller thrust even lower than the simple calculation up above. (more info: Theoretical Max Propeller Efficiency) And all this was being super generous, assuming a L/D of 20 for a vehicle as aerodynamically ugly as an 18 wheeler. For something that boxy, without adding a bunch of fairings, you'd be looking at an L/D well under 10. What this really goes to show is that flying takes a lot of power. That's why we only use airplanes when we need to get somewhere in a hurry. If you have the time, ground transportation is much more economical. (And of course, trains are even more economical than trucks, and boats and ships are even more economical, yet.)

Why did Tim Walz put female tampons and pads in the boys washroom? I have to say, this is one of the stranger tempests in a teapot I've seen in a while. The reality seems like such a mundane law (albeit very beneficial) that I’m surprised it’s managed to draw this much attention. But while most of the manufactured controversy came out of the right-wing, some left-wing responses have also been a bit more rationalization after the fact rather than what the law originally intended, and based more around conjecture than what's actually going on in Minnesota (i.e. it didn't have anything to do with logistics). So first – the civics lessons. Tim Walz didn't write this law. He didn't campaign on it or provide a draft for the legislature to act on. The law was originally sponsored by Sandra Feist in the Minnesota House, in a standalone bill, HF 44 , and then got included in the much larger Education Finance Bill, HF 2497. After going through the full process in the Minnesota House and Senate, the Education Finance Bill was eventually approved by majorities in both chambers, and so Tim Walz signed it into law. But this whole initiative of providing menstrual products to student was never something that Walz himself led. The main purpose of the law originally proposed by Feist is to provide menstrual products to students. This isn't some revolutionary idea new to Minnesota. There are similar laws on the books in 28 states and D.C. to address what some describe as "period poverty". According to Period Products in Schools, 1 in 4 students struggle to afford such products. And one study of a program in NYC found a 2.4% increase in attendance when free period products were offered to students. As one of the students who testified in the Minnesota House during a hearing on the legislation put it, "We cannot learn while we are leaking" (source: Minnesota may soon OK free menstrual products in schools. These teens led the way). ABOVE SOURCE: Period Products in Schools - Alliance for Period Supplies If you want to read the law for yourself, go to the full text of HF2497. It's easy to find the relevant portions. Just do a search for 'menstrual'. Here's the main portion: ARTICLE 1 GENERAL EDUCATION Section 1. [121A.212] ACCESS TO MENSTRUAL PRODUCTS. A school district or charter school must provide students with access to menstrual products at no charge. The products must be available to all menstruating students in restrooms regularly used by students in grades 4 to 12 according to a plan developed by the school district. For purposes of this section, "menstrual products" means pads, tampons, or other similar products used in connection with the menstrual cycle. There's another passage specifying that the budget for this will be "$2 times the adjusted pupil units of the school district for the school year", and another passage including these menstrual products in a list of allowed purposes for "Total operating capital revenue". Note that there's no mandate that tampons have to be supplied in the boys restroom. However, the language was gender neutral, allowing for discretion at the local levels for schools to implement this law. And that gender neutral language was on purpose. According to Feist, the sponsor of the original bill: While the vast majority of the period products will be used in the girls’ bathrooms, the decision was made to structure the bill as gender-inclusive in order to ensure that trans and nonbinary students who menstruate would have equal access to the products they need. SOURCE: Yes, Tim Walz signed a law requiring Minnesota public schools to provide free tampons in school bathrooms Also, as noted in the article, Why Republicans are calling Walz 'Tampon Tim' — and why Democrats embrace it, there was opposition to this gender inclusivity when "Some Minnesota Republicans initially tried to limit the initiative to female-assigned and gender-neutral bathrooms, but were unsuccessful." However, it's interesting to note that the Republican who proposed that amendment did go on to support the final bill, as he felt the overall issue was important, and not worth killing over that compromise. It’s also worth pointing out that schools are free to come up with their own plans to implement the law. According to an editorial from the Minnesota based Star Tribune, A reality check on the ‘Tampon Tim’ meme: At Anoka-Hennepin, the state’s largest school district, the free products are not found in traditional male-only bathrooms, a spokesman said. But they are provided for free to all in “nongendered bathrooms,” girls’ bathrooms or from health staffers. I can't say that absolutely no schools in Minnesota have provided tampons in the boys room, but if the largest school district in the state isn't doing so, it's obviously not a requirement of the law, so long as transgender students can still receive menstrual products if they need them. So basically, Tim Walz signed a large law that had a bunch of different sections dealing with multiple aspects of education funding. Among these was a requirement to provide tampons to students for free, which seems utterly reasonable to me. The language was made specifically gender neutral, allowing individual schools to implement the law as they saw fit, so long as they were still complying and supporting all students who needed menstrual products, which also seems pretty reasonable to me. And just to be clear, the law doesn't actually force schools to provide tampons in the boys room, and as proven in practice, at least one school district cited in the news hasn't.

What accidents or incidents have you personally had with deep fryers? Back when I was in high school, I got a job at KFC. There was a certain minimum level for the shortening in the pressure fryers, but they never actually gave us any formal training on proper technique to add more. The method I developed for myself was to cut off a chunk of shortening (it was solid at room temperature), then stab that chunk with the knife, and lower it down into the fryer. That seemed better to me than just throwing the chunk in there and having the hot grease splash. Well, one day, I had a just gotten a big chunk of shortening over the fryer when it fell off of the knife, and sent a huge splash of grease up at my head. I managed to turn to the side and close my eyes, but the grease got half of my face. I immediately went to the sink in the kitchen, and began running cold water over my face. The manager didn't seem to quite know what to do, and couldn't get a hold of my parents, so eventually, somebody gave me a ride home. When I did get home, my parents were out in the yard working (why they never heard the phone – this was a bit before cell phones), and were quite surprised to see me, especially with half my face burnt. So they immediately threw me into the car and drove me to the ER. The ER took me in right away (no waiting around like when you've merely got the sniffles), took me straight to a room, and then promptly treated me with nothing fancier than cold washcloths. Really, that was the only treatment – a basin of ice water with a few washcloths soaking in it, that my mom would swap out when the one on my face started to warm up too much. After a couple hours to draw out as much heat as possible, they sent me on my way with referrals for follow ups. Over the next few days, my face started to look bad. Luckily, it was mostly 'just' second degree burns. But once those blisters started popping and oozing puss all over my face, I was not a pretty sight. One of those referrals was a plastic surgeon, but the only real treatment I needed was bacitracin to prevent infection. All this happened just a couple weeks before graduation. Any open wounds had mostly healed in time, but the skin was still pretty tender, and I was supposed to keep out of the sun. So, I went everywhere with a wide brimmed hat, and avoided sitting out under the sun for all of the graduation rehearsals. I also avoided shaving, so I had that just wrong 17 year old level of stubble – more scruffy than rugged. A couple friends and I had also planned a cross country road trip right after graduation, which meant upgrading our provisional drivers licenses to full licenses, so we wouldn't have any restrictions driving during the trip. Oh man was that a horrible drivers license photo, between the scruff, red face, and completely unkempt hair once I took off the wide brimmed hat. Whenever anybody complained about a bad drivers license photo, I always had them beat (and they always agreed). Thankfully, I only developed a few minor scars, that weren't even that obvious when I was clean shaven, but are now completely hidden by my (adult) beard. Anyway, I was more careful adding shortening after that. I even got workman’s comp out of it.

Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs? It depends on what you mean by 'walking'. It's also a bit cloudy because of the incompleteness of the fossil record. Let's address the definition of 'walking', first. Take a look at this video of a modern day creature (i.e. not our ancestor, and not even particularly closely related): I think it’s reasonable to say that it's walking along the coral reef, using its fins much like legs. And the truth is, walking underwater is a useful form of locomotion. Handfish and frogfish are also quite well known for walking underwater. And it seems that in our own ancestors, walking underwater came first, before any of them ever tried to crawl up onto a mud bank. I found an article that goes into great detail on the origin of tetrapods, The Fish–Tetrapod Transition: New Fossils and Interpretations. Here's a figure from that article, showing the relationships of species know from fossils, along with the general timeframe of when tetrapods evolved: ABOVE: Stratigraphic table of Late Devonian and Early Carboniferous with cladogram of tetrapodomorphs superimposed to show distribution in time. Broad bars show known range, narrow bars show possible range where exact dating is not available. Based on Ahlberg et al. (2008) SOURCE: The Fish–Tetrapod Transition: New Fossils and Interpretations Note that most of those are side branches, not our direct ancestors, so they're really only giving us a general idea of what our ancestors would have been like, not precise snapshots. Still, the first creatures to walk would have been along those lines. Here's another figure, with less animals, but with pictures of the ones that were included, including diagrams of their forelimbs: SOURCE: The origin of tetrapods - Understanding Evolution So, the first of our ancestors to walk underwater probably would have been something along the lines of Panderichthys. The first of our ancestors to spend an appreciable amount of time walking on land would have been something along the lines of Acanthostega. Though keep in mind the timeframes from the earlier figure, and that Acanthostega was living well after the actual first creatures to become so terrestrial. With recent finds over the past few decades, the current fossil record actually already is a lot more complete than when I was a kid. But there are still plenty of transitional species left to be found. I'm excited for scientists to find them so that I can learn about them.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? Yes. And Trump could beat Harris. Presidential elections in the past 30 years have all been relatively close. Roughly half the votes will go to either candidate, plus or minus a few percent that decides who will win (and a few more percent to third party candidates). And of course, that whole process gets filtered through the electoral college, so a candidate doesn't even need a majority of the popular vote to win the election. ABOVE SOURCE: United States presidential election - Wikipedia This year will be no different. Trump will get around half the vote. Harris will get around half the vote. Whoever performs best in the swing states will win the overall election. Sure, you've got plenty of people right now making 'guarantees' about who will win. And given that it's really a binary choice, a lot of those people will inevitably end up picking the eventual winner. But it doesn't mean they actually had any better insight than the rest of us. It means they just got lucky by calling the coin toss. I think we can safely predict, at least, that Robert Kennedy is not going to win. Side note: I don't mean to discount polling as worthless. I think it still is useful and valid as long as you understand it's limitations. It's just that polling can't tell you much when elections are decided by less than the polling margin of error. Another side note: This question is from 2016, but for obvious reasons, it's taken on a new found relevance.

Why is the news about the solar eclipse still in the news two days afterwards? Because it was really damn cool, and many of us who saw it are still looking up follow up stories. And considering that those of us who saw it include several high population areas across North America and big cities close enough for people to make day trips out of it (a few million people total traveled to see the eclipse), that’s a lot of potentially interested people. Getting to personally see a total eclipse really is a pretty rare thing, potentially once in a lifetime. Sure, total eclipses happen every year and a half or so, but the path of totality is relatively narrow, and the Earth is pretty big, so most people aren’t all that close to most total eclipses. Getting a total eclipse that passed right over so many major population centers and so close to so many others is going to drive a lot of interest in those locations. How long did it take for humans to evolve from monkeys? Why are there no living monkeys that have evolved into humans? Although I usually avoid answering the A.I. Quora Prompt Generator (QPG) questions, there are already several other answers to this one that all took a different approach than I would have, so let me add my 2¢. Trying to pin specific numbers to this answer comes down to what you want to call a monkey, and whether you think monkeys should be monophyletic, paraphyletic, or polyphyletic. It doesn't change the actual evolutionary history of humans, just the semantics of what's a monkey and what isn't. Here's a diagram to help understand those terms: ABOVE SOURCE: Monophyletic, Polyphyletic, & Paraphyletc Taxa Here are the written definitions from that page: ...a monophyletic taxon is defined as one that includes the most recent common ancestor of a group of organisms, and all of its descendents [as in (a)]. ...a paraphyletic taxon [is] one that includes the most recent common ancestor, but not all of its descendents [as in (c)]. A polyphyletic taxon is defined as one that does not include the common ancestor of all members of the taxon [as in (b)]. Now, here's a broad evolutionary history of primates: ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982212008068 So, the semantic question comes down to, what on that diagram is a monkey? If it's only the New World monkeys and Old World monkeys but not the 'Early simians', then monkeys are a polyphyletic group. That would mean we humans evolved from simians, but not monkeys, so the QPG's question can't be answered. If you think those early simians are themselves monkeys, but want to split apes off into something separate, then monkeys would be a paraphyletic group. Our lineage, the apes, would have split off from the monkeys around 36 million years ago, which would make the answer to the QPG's question 36 million years. (Though to be clear, you could say the same thing about all the other modern apes, as well. For example, that it's taken chimpanzees 36 million years to evolve from monkeys.) But if you think monkeys should be a monophyletic group, then everything descended from those early simians should be counted as monkeys. And then the question is back to being unanswerable, since we humans would still be monkeys, ourselves. My most recent monkey ancestors would be my mom and dad. I personally descended from monkeys in the late 1970s. That last point does address the QPG's last question. The living monkeys that evolved into humans are us. And the reason why no other monkeys or apes are evolving to be more like us now is because of the Competitive exclusion principle. We humans already occupy the niche of being hyper social technological primates. So other primates need to specialize in other niches that don't compete with ours. Anyway, while the question did come from the QPG, I have seen real people sincerely ask similar questions, so I think this was worth answering. And although the answer comes down partially to semantics, the evolutionary history of people in that diagram up above is still accurate no matter which creatures you think are monkeys or not.
